notes.headline: Ross Stores: comparable sales up 8% on rising traffic and EPS of $1.91 tops guidance; full-year outlook raised to $8.75–$8.84
notes.takeaway: Sales rose 12% to $6.3 billion, comparable sales grew 8% on top of 7% last year, and EPS of $1.91 beat both the company’s $1.75–$1.83 guidance and the $1.87 consensus. Ross kept its holiday-quarter outlook and raised full-year EPS guidance to $8.75–$8.84, yet the shares slipped 3% the next day.
results: Ross Stores reported sales of $6.3 billion for the quarter ended October 31, up 12% from $5.6 billion, with comparable store sales up 8% against a 7% gain a year earlier, driven mainly by more customer visits. Net income rose to $606 million from $512 million and earnings per share to $1.91 from $1.58, above the company’s guidance and the analysts’ $1.87.

Operating margin was 12.3%, up 0.7 points and above the company’s plan of 11.7% to 12.0%. The company opened 51 stores in the quarter — 41 Ross and 10 dd’s DISCOUNTS — completing its 2026 plan of 115 new locations.

For the first nine months sales rose 15% to $18.5 billion, comparable sales grew 11% and EPS rose to $6.59 from $4.61, a figure that includes about $0.60 from refunds of tariffs paid under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act booked in the second quarter. Ross bought back $319 million of stock in the quarter and remains on track for $1.275 billion this year.
mgmt: Chief executive Jim Conroy said results beat expectations despite tougher comparisons, crediting marketing initiatives that are attracting more customers, a strong mix of brands at low prices and an improved store experience, and said the market share gains reinforce his confidence.

For the fourth quarter Ross kept its outlook for comparable sales growth of 4% to 5%, against a 9% gain last year, and EPS of $2.16 to $2.25, up 8% to 13%. Full-year EPS guidance rose to $8.75–$8.84, including the roughly $0.60 tariff-refund benefit. The board declared a quarterly dividend of $0.445.
view: Ross is having the kind of year off-price retailers dream about. Comparable sales up 11% over nine months for a chain with more than 2,200 stores is exceptional, and the fact that traffic rather than higher prices is driving it says Ross is taking customers from department stores and mid-tier apparel chains, not merely benefiting from inflation. It also says the strategy under Jim Conroy — who joined from Ollie’s in 2025 and brought a sharper marketing approach and more recognisable brands into the stores — is working faster than the market expected.

The margin line is the second piece of good news. Off-price margins were squeezed in 2024 and 2025 by freight, wages and tariff costs; a 70 basis-point improvement while still opening more than a hundred stores a year shows that the extra sales are dropping through to profit. The tariff refunds flatter this year’s total but not the quarter, and the underlying growth in operating income is what supports the share price.

The challenge now is arithmetic. Fourth-quarter guidance of 4% to 5% comparable growth against a 9% gain last year is sensible, and Ross has a long record of guiding low and beating, but next year it will be lapping double-digit growth and a one-off $0.60 tariff benefit. Investors paying around 25 times earnings need to believe the share gains are durable rather than a cyclical shift as consumers trade down. This quarter is evidence for durability; the first half of 2027 will be the real test.
notes.watch: Watch holiday comparable sales against the 4%–5% guide, the 2027 outlook in March including how management frames the tariff-refund comparison, and the pace of store openings.
